speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as to-day has been set apart for the official recognition of the birthday of His Majesty, King George VI, I am sure hon. members would desire to have an expression of their wishes extended to His Majesty. I have spoken to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), and he and I have agreed upon a resolution which, we believe, hon. members would be prepared to support. I would therefore move, seconded by the leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition:
That a humble address be sent to His Majesty, King George VI, in the following words:
"To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
On this day set apart for the official celebration of Your Majesty's birthday, we. the members of the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, desire respectfully to extend our loyal greetings and heartfelt good wishes to Your Majesty.

The devotion to duty and high courage which you have continuously shown throughout the present war have been an inspiration to the people of Canada, to the peoples of the British commonwealth, and, indeed, to those of all of the united nations.
We pray that Divine Providence may continue. to guide and. protect Your Majesty and that you may be given strength to meet, at all times, the great responsibilities of your high office.
May you witness an early triumph of the forces of freedom and share with your peoples everywhere, for many years to come, the blessings of a just and enduring peace."

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to second the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that a humble address be sent to His Majesty, King George VI, I would echo the sentiments so well expressed in the Prime Minister's motion. I think all hon. members will recall at once the visit of Their Majesties in 1939 and the beneficial effect of that visit, in a greater understanding between the parts of the empire and the Anglo-Saxon nations generally.
During the very trying times through which the empire, and particularly Great Britain herself, has passed, the tender sympathy and understanding of Their Majesties can be recalled to-day by all of us with a great deal of pride and satisfaction. In the days of trial through which this nation and this empire are going, and will go, the bond of sentimental attachment to the monarchy and to Britain has, I believe, never been stronger. I take this opportunity of thanking the Prime Minister for the privilege of seconding this motion.

subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: We also support the motion of congratulation to His Majesty the King. The monarchy is the symbol of unity among the peoples of the British commonwealth of nations, and, as such, we are glad to support the resolution.

We have put first in our work the importance of coming to an agreement "with the dominions", Sir Archibald said of the government's civil aviation plans. maintopic: EXCHANGE OF NOTES BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT OF THE UNITED KINGDOM AND THE REPUBLIC OF CZECHOSLOVAKIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: EXCHANGE OF NOTES BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT OF THE UNITED KINGDOM AND THE REPUBLIC OF CZECHOSLOVAKIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity of referring to the exchange of notes between the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, Mr. Eden, and the foreign minister of the Czechoslovak republic, Mr. Masaryk, which took place on August 5 of last year. The statement I am making has reference to the Munich agreement. It is a communication that I am glad to have the opportunity of making to the house before Doctor Benes, the President of the Republic of Czechoslovakia, arrives. I had intended making it at an earlier stage of the session, but an opportunity has not presented itself.
In his note, Mr. Eden stated that in order to avoid any possible misunderstanding, he desired to declare that as Germany had deliberately destroyed the arrangements concerning Czechoslovakia reached at Munich in 1938, his government regarded themselves as free from any engagements in this respect. He stated further that at the final settlement of the Czechoslovak frontiers to be reached at the end of the war, the British government would not be influenced by any changes effected in and since 1938.
The Canadian government has not considered it necessary to enter into a similar exchange with the Czechoslovak government, since Canada was not a party to the Munich agreement. I am glad, however, to take this occasion to state thaf the Canadian government fully shares the view of the United Kingdom government that the Munich agreement is void.
It is not without interest that, when our government amended the defence of Canada regulations in April of 1941, in order to remove any possibility of Czechoslovaks being regarded as enemy nationals, the amendment stated that for the purposes of these regulations, Czechoslovakia means "Czechoslovakia as it existed on the first day of January, 1938." It is the earnest wish of our country that the day will not be far removed when the brave people of Czechoslovakia will again enjoy those liberties which enabled them to make their very real contribution to the democratic life and culture of Europe.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, now that my honourable colleagues seem to have finished asking questions, I rise to a question of privilege, based on an article which has been published by a newspaper which specializes in not ^informing its readers, or in misinforming them, and which wrote a very bitter article against Mr. Aberhart last week, before his ashes were cold. The article is entitled, " Less Talking, Please," and refers to the speeches made in the house by hon. members for Leeds (Mr. Ful-ford) and Wellington North (Mr. Blair). They are quotations, but I understand the ration limit of gags has been exhausted, and that the manufacturer is out of stock. The article goes on to say:
There is an increasingly large number of citizens throughout the country who will heartily endorse Doctor Blair's sentiments.
And for your information, my name is mentioned in the first part of the article.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL DAILY STAR OF MAY 28
speechtext: What paper?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL DAILY STAR OF MAY 28
speechtext:
The Montreal Daily Star, a paper which either does not inform its readers or misinforms them. The article continues:
Parliament was not established in order to provide any member with an entirely erroneous idea of his own importance, to talk interminably in debate, particularly when what he says is for the main part obviously not intended for any other purpose than to draw the limelight upon himself.
I have been fighting for the underdog and for the people, but when hon. members express ideas which I desire to express, I am perfectly satisfied because I believe in the law of least effort. The article continues:
It may become necessary to amend the rules of debate if the privilege of free speech continues to be so flagrantly and insensately abused. This abuse is all the more irritating because it is confined to a very small number of members. We wonder, by the way, if it would be so persistent if the privilege of franking Hansard to the members' constituents were to be cancelled.
I suggest that a copy of Hansard be sent daily to each reader of the Montreal Star so that he may be informed, because the parliamentary reports of the Montreal Star are pure rot. I quote:
We urge that some action of an. effective nature be taken. They manage to control time-wasters elsewhere without any outcry as to the
Privilege-Mr. Pouliot

curtailment of the privilege of free speech, and it certainly ought to be possible for the parliament of Canada to do the same.
Here is a loyalist paper that is suggesting that we do the same thing as is done in Germany. My work is hard; I am doing a painful and a painstaking task, and I should like to ask something of the government. Parliamentary secretaries have been appointed and I wonder if I could not have three. I should like to have the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), if he can be spared by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie); I should like to have the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair), if he can be spared from his groundhogs-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL DAILY STAR OF MAY 28
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL DAILY STAR OF MAY 28
speechtext: The question of privilege is something that should be raised rarely by an hon. member and only if he has been libelled or an aspersion has been cast upon him. As a matter of privilege the member has the right to deny what has been said about him, but he can refer only to the article which has appeared in the newspaper and which should be placed on the table of the house. His denial may be given but he is not entitled to enter into an argument or to comment at length on what has been published. All he is entitled to do is deny what has been said in the editorial and to state his position as shortly as it can be stated.

Mr. Fulford pointed out that if all members took as much time as Mr. Pouliot did, the house would have to sit twenty-four hours a day three hundred and sixty-five days a year, and said that members were becoming exasperated. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 1, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
2. Pay and allowances, $238,023,232.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take up what I am afraid will be considerable time of the committee to discuss a matter which was brought up yesterday by a large number of members, namely, that of the commissioning of aircrew in the Royal Canadian Air Force. This is a question which has aroused much public attention and has been discussed and debated a great deal throughout the country during the past year. I must ask the committee to give me some little time in which to make this explanation because it is a complicated matter and one in which a number of interests are involved as well as, apart from the broader interests, the individuals who are entitled to the promotion which they desire.
It will be remembered that when we were discussing the war appropriation bill last year this question of commissioning was brought to my attention, and I expressed myself somewhat forcibly as being strongly in favour of the commissioning of all aircrew. I have not changed my opinion in that regard, although I must admit that circumstances have been such that it has not been possible to carry out the policy to the extent I should have liked. It will be necessary for me to go into some detail and to give some account of the background of the story of commissioning.
When the joint air training plan agreement was signed in December, 1939, there was only passing mention of commissioning. It was said that pilots and observers could be commissioned in certain numbers, and I think it was arranged that agreement would be made as to the percentage and numbers of aircrew which would be commissioned. It was not until February, 1940, that any concrete plan of commissioning was laid before the partners to the agreement. At a meeting of the supervisory board, which as the committee knows is the board which supervises the administration by Canada of the empire training agreement, it was agreed that commissioning of pilots and observers would be on the basis as expressed by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), that is, the top one-third who had

War Appropriation-Air Services
passed their examination would receive commissions on graduation and the remaining seventeen per cent, in order to bring the total up to fifty per cent, would be commissioned on active ' service provided they were recommended at the time of their graduation.
That referred only to pilots and observers. There was no provision made for the commissioning of wireless operator air gunners or of straight air gunners. As a matter of fact straight air gunners were not being turned out to any extent in the early days. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that this arrangement was made in February, 1940, before any aircrew had begun training, in fact I imagine before any aircrew had been enlisted. The first aircrew began their training in April, 1940. This procedure existed for some little time, as I shall presently show.
A year after, in February, 1941, at the instance of the Canadian government, or rather of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who felt that it would1 be extremely difficult to obtain recruits for wireless operator air gunners, who had a very long and tedious course to follow, unless some recognition were given at least to the persons who came out best in their examinations, it was agreed that two per cent of the wireless operator air gunners should obtain commissions. Even then there was no question of commissions for straight air gunners. A month or so later it was decided that five per cent of the wireless operator air gunners, instead of two per cent, should be commissioned. There were still no commissions for the air gunners. Then, during the course of my visit overseas in 1941, I took up this matter of commissioning of air gunners and wireless operator air gunners with the air ministry, and as a result of discussions at that time it was agreed that ten per cent of the wireless operator air gunners would be commissioned on graduation and ten per cent later on in operations, making a total of twenty per cent. With respect to air gunners, five per cent would be commissioned on graduation and fifteen per cent on operations, making a total of twenty per cent.
That brought it down to April, 1942, when I stated in this chamber, on the appropriations, that I favoured one hundred per cent commissions. Then came the empire training air conference in May of 1942. At that conference Canada proposed to its partners that all aircrew be commissioned. The partners did not agree either to the proposition that all aircrews be commissioned or, alternatively, as a second suggestion, that all aircrews be given what might be called an intermediate rank- ensign or cadet or flight officer, call it what
you will-which would be the intermediate probationary rank between the non-commissioned officer and the commissioned officer. Such a rank is now in existence in the United States army air corps, and presently I will give some indication of how it works.
Before the minister passes to another matter, what were the reasons advanced by the partners for failure to commission those in the aircrews?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have a long story to tell on that. So, by way of a compromise-which is in accordance with the genius of British institutions- it was decided - Canada having refused to continue the old system-on 33 per cent on graduation and 17 per cent in the field. So that, as was stated by the hon. member for Rosedale, the agreement, appendix 3, page 11, contains this clause:
1. Commissioning- . . .
(a) All pilots, observers, navigators and air bombers who are considered suitable according to the standards of the government of Canada and who are recommended for commissions will be commissioned.
It goes on to give the percentages with respect to wireless operator air gunners and to air gunners. That is to say, our partners agreed that we should commission whom we wanted but asked us to establish a certain standard, and that we agreed to do. We receded from our position of commissioning everybody and we adopted a formula which was first suggested by tfie United Kingdom, that all aircrew who were commissionable should be commissioned. That formula might or might not mean a great deal-" all aircrew who were commissionable should be commissioned." Therefore we said, " That is all right, but we had better have some kind of yardstick and some kind of standard," and we did establish such a yardstick and such a standard, to which I will presently refer, and which in effect has resulted in the granting of a very much larger number of commissions on graduation.
My principal anxiety during all the time this agitation was proceeding for commissioning on graduation was with respect to the poor lads who were overseas. Not so much was being heard about them in Canada in those days, partly because we had not our own squadrons, partly because our publicity had not been properly arranged, and to a certain extent, too, because we had not been in operation to the extent that we have been recently, and not so many of our men were returning. So that the agitation in Canada largely had for its objective

War Appropriation-Air Services
the commissioning of men on graduation. I felt that that would be grossly unfair to the lads who had been over for a year or so. They were my first consideration; and in discussing this subject with the United Kingdom-in which reams of paper were consumed in dispatches-I said: At least give commissions to the seventeen per cent who are recommended on graduation-at least seek them out and see that they get their commissions. Well, that did not seem to work. There are reasons. I am not attempting in any way to blame, as somebody expressed it, Great Britain or anybody for this. It is very difficult in the course of operations for a commanding officer-who after all has the say in spite of the fact that there was a recommendation on graduation-to follow all these things through, and I am absolutely certain that ninety-five per cent of the Royal Air Force commanding officers did not know anything of the agreements made at the time of the joint air training plan, or of the ruling of the supervisory board that seventeen per cent should be commissioned, or that John Jones from Saskatoon had been recommended for consideration for a commission when he started in on active service. He saw John Jones, but he probably never saw Jphn Jones's file, and did not know anything about it. The result is that those commissions were not coming through. Presently I will give a statement of the numbers in 1941, 1942 and 1943. So that something had to be done about it, and we wrote into the agreement of 1942 something which hon. members, particularly those who know something of military affairs, will agree was a most unusual provision. It was to do away with the recommendation of the officer commanding, and in some respects take the matter of commissioning into our own hands. The clause reads:
(c) Normally, the initiative in recommending an airman for a commission will rest with his commanding officer, but an airman may apply to be recommended, and, if his application is endorsed and forwarded by his commanding officer, it will receive the same consideration as if it had been initiated by the latter.
An application for a commission by an airman of the Royal Canadian Air Force, even if it is not endorsed-
That is, even if the commanding officer does not agree that the man should be commissioned.
-will be forwarded through the usual channels. . . .
It goes all the way up from the commanding officer to the group, from the group to

the command, from the command to the air ministry, and the air ministry have a look at it and, if they still do not want it, it goes to Royal Canadian Air Force headquarters, and these headquarters will be provided with all relevant documents and will arrange for the candidate to appear before a selection board convened by the air officer-in-chief, R.C.A.F. overseas. In other words, if the application of a Canadian had not been considered or had been turned down, even though he is in the Royal Air Force, even though he may be in the middle east, or in Burma; no matter where he is, subject always to the difficulties of communication and transportation, he may appeal to the Canadian board to see whether or not he will get his commission. We also provided that there would be a review of all aircrew within two months after the signing of this agreement. That was in order to give our boys overseas at least an opportunity of having their commissionable qualities judged by Canadians. I have been asked how this works.

The minister said he
wrote that into the agreement.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Does that mean that the other parties concurred?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The other parties concurred, but this refers only to Canada. This gives the conditions of service of aircrew of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I do not know whether Australia and1 New Zealand have since written something similar into their agreement, but I rather suspect that they are following our procedure.
That was the situation in June, 1942. We proceeded to establish the standard which was referred to. We entirely disagree with the system, a sort of casual, fortuitous system, whereby the top thirty-three per cent of any class would obtain commissions. That did not work well. There were some classes much better than others. There were men who were up against strong competition who were much better than men in a weaker class and they did not obtain their commissions. We found that it was a most illogical way of doing it. We therefore set up our standards very much after the system of university examinations. We said that if a man gets sixty per cent in each subject and seventy per cent over all, whether there be a hundred or ten in the class, it does not matter, if he gets these marks he will receive his commission. The result has been a considerable increase

War Appropriation-Air Services
in the number of commissions. I signed selection board papers last week from three different boards in regard to pilots. In one board 76 per cent obtained commissions, in another over 80 per cent; and I have known a board wherein there were only two Canadians,
I must say, with 100 per cent, and another where there was 90 per cent. So that the 33 per cent is wiped out.

Is there any examining
board that will ensure uniformity?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The questions are pretty
much the same and the syllabus is also much the same. The board is made up usually of the chief flying instructor and probably the chief instructor, ground. Ground subjects, flying subjects and other matters are dealt with. We go back now, in order to get these marks, and follow a man right from the first school he joins, from the I.TS. He does not fly in the I.T.S., but he gets marks there for ground subjects, character and leadership, and at the elementary flying school he gets marks for the same subjects plus flying. Originally the judgment and perhaps-I say this without wishing to be offensive to anyone-the prejudice of the commanding officer or of someone ini the last class in which the man passed was brought to bear. That is inevitable in matters of this kind. But now with the yardstick we have, form 211, wherein all a man's qualities are taken into account and marks are recorded from every school to which he goes, we obtain a pretty good idea of his value by the time he gets through after he has been with us over a year; and on that basis his marks are allotted and he gets his commission, or he does not get it, as the case may be. So far as its effect on the number of commissions is concerned, it has materially increased the number of commissions on graduation.
With regard to overseas, continual representations were being made, and I will give the figures to show that there has been a vast improvement. In November, 1941, there were 25 commissions and in December, 58. In 1942 these were the commissions: January, 32; February, 49; March, 65; April, 64; May, 32; June, 112; July, 44; August, 127; September, 102; October 74. Then in 1943: January, 228; February, 239; March, 167; April, 231; and I expect over 300 in May. That is not yet enough. We have many more to get. I believe, however, that the system is getting into its stride and we hope that within a short time pretty nearly all those who have been overseas for some time and those on active operations will have received commissions or reasons will be given by the commanding
72537-207i
officer why they have not received' them. When the reason is given it will be a matter for the Royal Canadian Air Force to decide whether it is valid or not. If the commanding officer makes a report indicating that the man is not in his opinion commissionable, and gives valid reasons for that opinion, I do not know whether we would overrule him or not, but that would be a matter for the discretion of the Canadian board, sitting at Canadian headquarters in London.
Is the minister satisfied that this is the best arrangement that can be made?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would much prefer to get 100 and let it go at that; it would save much correspondence and trouble. But we are in the empire training agreement with our partners, and if you cannot get everything in any deal you get what you can. Moreover, this must not be lost sight of. The large proportion of our men are serving with the R.A.F. As it is now a very much larger percentage of our men have commissions. They will be in R.A.F. units and it does cause some embarrassment to the R.A.F. You will probably say that I should answer them, "Do as we do", and I will come to that in a moment. The fact is, however, that they have a staunch deep-rooted objection to coming to our point of view. At any rate, a great deal of embarrassment is created, and it must also cause embarrassment here. There are R.A.F., Australian, New Zealand and Canadian airmen graduating in the same schools in Canada. Our men are on the basis of 60, 60, 60 and 70-60 in three subjects and 70 over all. If they get that they get a commission. There might be some Australian, New Zealander or Englishman who had higher marks, but because he was not in the first third he would not get his commission. They do not like that, and some embarrassment is caused overseas. The house will say perhaps that I am getting unduly perturbed about embarrassing people, but I can feel for them although I do not sympathize with their point of view.
The only way to get over the embarrassment is to commission everyone in the aircrew.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are getting a much higher proportion both on graduation and in the field than before, though we have not been able to attain the objective we have aimed at. The reasons the R.A.F. oppose this system are these. The R.A.F. have made up their minds from experience that not more than fifty per cent are commissionable. That is to say,

War Appropriation-Air Services
out of a population of a certain number of people who join the aircrew, not more than fifty per cent will be fit to be officers.
Is there any reason for that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They say that is their
experience.

Is it experience or
tradition?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
According to tradition it would be much smaller than that. However, they say that is their experience.
They say that is their experience. I deny them the right to say that they have any more experience than we have. We have trained more men in this country for flying than they have. And if it is a question of training citizen soldiers I am inclined to agree with them; if they want to carry it out on the basis of a permanent force and a permanent army, they know more about that than we do. They are sticking to that basis, I think, when they lay down the broad general rule that not more than 50 per cent of the men who come in are fit to be officers.
The minister is speaking of aircrew only?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Exclusive of all except those on operations?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; that is everything. They say that of those who have the educational, mental and physical qualities to be aircrew, 50 per cent are fit to be officers and 50 per cent non-commissioned officers.
I hope that with very great respect you differed from them on that point.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will show you. I have in my hand a document which is edited by British Information. It is an agency of the British government. It is entitled "Officers and Non-Commissioned Officers of the R.A.F." I am taking up a lot of time of the committee, but I think the committee is interested in this question-
It is very important.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It says, and this is for American consumption no doubt:
Questions are frequently raised about the apparent disparity of rank between men who are flying and fighting aircraft.
Why are some of them commissioned officers and some of them airmen pilots? Why do some live in the officers' mess and some in the sergeants' mess? Why do some earn the

Distinguished Flying Cross, and some the Distinguished Flying Medal for acts of gallantry which are in the same category?
Such questions are natural, but the suggestion of a class element in the choice between officers and other ranks is based on a misconception of facts.
It is clear tbrougout the R.A.F. that class distinction has no influence in the selection of cadets for flying training.
There is no doubt about that:
All cadets are potential officers. All have a chance of securing a commission should they desire to be commissioned, and be judged fitted for holding a commission.
The young officer must rise on his own merits, and can come from any walk of life. Potential pilot officers and potential sergeant pilots start on the same level. Whatever the origin of the man he must enter the ranks of the R.A.F. as an aircraft hand under training, and win his "Wings" and possible commission by his industry. ability and daring.
If the entrant has the physical and mental equipment to handle and fight aircraft of modern war type and has also a certain standard of education, he is accepted for aircrew training and is graded as a cadet. Thereafter his future is entirely his own making.
At the other end of his training there must necessarily be a discrimination, for the flow of promotion to higher ranks in the service must go on, and must come from the pool of young pilots. In order to provide for the necessary numbers of flight commanders and officers of senior rank in a squadron, it is essential to find fifty young officers from every one hundred pilots.
Natural prudence dictates that more officers should not be made at the outset than are required. On the other hand it should be noted that there is never a time in the career of an airman pilot in which it can be said that he is "out of the running" for a commission.
There are also paragraphs to the effect that a great many of those in the Royal Air Force do not want commissions, that they are better off financially without them. It goes on to say:
In the battle of Britain fifty per cent of the fighter pilots who tackled the Luftwaffe over southeastern England were sergeants. To-day, when Hurricanes and Spitfires sweep out over the channel to meet the enemy in French skies, every other pilot of the raiding fighters is wearing the uniform of an N.C.O. beneath his flying suit.
. In the forefront of all bombing attacks on the enemy are sergeants, either as captains of aircraft or the majority of the crews. And scarcely a list of R.A.F. awards is issued that does not contain the name of many sergeants.
In the words of a commanding officer, who also flew in the old Royal Flying Corps: "It rvas always reckoned that sergeants were the backbone of the British army-I think the same can be said of the modern air force."

A sergeant would not be any poorer fighter if you gave him a commission.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He might be poorer financially according to this statement.

Would the minister explain why an officer receives flying pay of, I think, two dollars a day and the flight sergeant or sergeant pilot receives only seventy-five cents a day flying pay? Why is there not equality of payment there?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I really do not know. I
will look into that. To come down to our discussions with the Royal Air Force and the British Air Ministry, I told the Air Ministry that this matter would have to come up in the house. I said that I wanted to be fair to everybody and that I should like to have a statement of the position they took. I have it here. It is called an "Aide Memoire." This is from the United Kingdom. I will quote a few paragraphs from this and then from my reply if the committee is interested. This "Aide Memoire" states:
When commissioning of pilots ami observers first came to be considered it was estimated that no less than half the posts which graduates in these trades were designed to fill would need to be filled by commissioned officers and that accordingly a fifty per cent commissioning standard could safely be adopted, some 33 per cent to be commissioned on graduation and some 17 per cent after service.
This "Aide Memoire" is very recent. It is since the conference was held within the last month. It goes on to say:
When WO/AGs and AGs began to be needed in large numbers, position was (a) that qualification for these trades were more restricted than for pilots and observers and that candidates rejected for the latter trades could be accepted for the former-
That is quite true. It goes on:
-and (b) that a smaller proportion of posts for which WO/AGs and AGs were destined were posts which justified commissioned rank.
These, I take it, were posts on the establishment. It goes on to say:
It was necessary therefore not only to fix lower rates of pay for WO/AGs and AGs but also to fix lower commissioning percentage for them. Percentage fixed rvas 20 per cent (10 on graduation and 10 after service for WO/AGs and 5 and 15 per cent for AGs) and even this was not strictly justifiable on establishment grounds.
Experience shows that these percentages did not in fact operate to prevent commissioning of air crew's who were clearly fit to be commissioned. On the contrary the difficulty was to get enough aircrews recommended to keep percentages filled, and this despite the fact that the monthly reports had to be rendered on all aircrews eligible for commissions. Had it been otherwise steps would have been taken to increase percentages.
Perhaps the committee will be interested in the reply I made to these two paragraphs. I am dealing specifically with the "Aide
Memoire" paragraph by paragraph. The first plan in 1939 was that no aircrew would be commissioned. We insisted that we would not get the proper type unless we promised commissions particularly when we were competing in the open field with the army and navy since conscription did not exist in Canada. It had been said that we thought we should have more commissions in order to carry out our policy. I now quote from my reply to the Air Ministry:
Canada had proposed that all aircrew be commissioned, but in the light of strong opposition from the partners, and being unwilling to disturb the happy relations which had heretofore existed between all parties, agreed to the formula first suggested by the United Kingdom, and finally acceded to by all concerned, namely, "that all who were commissionable were to be commissioned", and on that basis undertook to set up its own standards for commissions. (This was done by substituting the "merit system" for the "quota system".)
The standard established by Canada was based on the marks obtained by the pupil in every stage of his training. The marks considered necessary to qualify for commission on graduation were 00 per cent in each subject and 70 per cent over all.
I went on:
The difference between us is simply this. You persist in the view that an arbitrary figure of 50 per cent of graduates, namely 33 per cent on graduation and 17 per cent after service in the field, are in fact commissionable and no more. We, on the other hand, contend that all those who by the marks obtained in their training and that extends over a period of a year, under the closest possible observation, show that they have commissionable qualities should be commissioned.
We do not hold to the view that an increased number of commissions on graduation will lower the standard in any appreciable degree, any more than an increased number of commissions granted for good service in the field will lower the efficiency of the units or of the individual personnel. On the contraiy, we believe that our "merit system" has many advantages over your "quota system" which, however well it may operate with R.A.F. personnel, definitely militates aeainst initiative, ambition and consequently efficiency in our men.
Still on this ouota system. Possiblv our friends in the British Air Ministry fail to see that although in Great Britain with their population and with the class distinctions that exist there, twenty-five per cent, let us say, or perhaps thirty per cent of the population are of a higher cultural and educational standard than the others, that condition does not exist in this country, where I would say eighty per cent if not ninety per cent of those who enter aircrew are of the same cultural or educational standard. I am not criticizing in any way the British system; it may apply perfectly there and may be good for them, but does not apply to us. Our boys have about the same class background. if you want to put it in that way;

War Appropriation-Air Services
they have the same school background, the same athletic background, and they can mix with one another without any class distinctions. I am not saying that in justification or otherwise of the system in force in the United Kingdom, but I think it should be said, and we have so expressed ourselves.

I think that is quite
right.
But the fact is that our boys are being penalized because of their system, because if we grant more commissions than they do we embarrass them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We are not being penalized; we are getting more and more commissions. We are coming up.
According to a return tabled in the house, seventy-five per cent of the men-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: But we have improved a great deal since February 28, when those figures were given. The thing is working better now.

Has the minister any
later figures?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
1 gave the figures for
March and April. For some reason or other March was a bad month, but April was pretty good and I think May was better. There were other reasons given, and I am again speaking the British piece:
If all aircrews were to be commissioned, situation would soon arise that those of superior ability or whose duties require them to exercise command over others would need to be promoted to flight lieutenant. In that event difficulty of choice will not have been disposed of but will merely have been transferred to the next higher stage in rank.
There is one paragraph here in particular which I think the committee should hear:
When their representative agreed in Ottawa in June, 1942, to abolish percentage basis of commissioning for pilot, navigator and bomber categories, they were under the impression that no lowering of commissioning standards was contemplated and they expected therefore that no material increase in number of commissioned would result. Nevertheless it was felt that percentage basis for pilots, navigators and bombers would have a psychological value.
This is a reversion to the idea that fifty per cent were all that were fit to be officers. Then the committee will remember that there was some statement about a review being made every month, with a report being made on each member of aircrew. I took some objection to that, and said:
Canada has some doubts as to the efficacy of the monthly review referred to since of the nine hundred persons whose names had been
lMr. Power.}
presented to the air ministry in November, 1942, as having been recommended on graduation for commissions in the field after actual operational experience the United Kingdom high commissioner reported in January, 1943, that 172 had already become casualties and 200 had not as yet been traced.
In order to bring this thing to a head, last November we took a list of nine hundred men who had been recommended, and who would be in this seventeen per cent, and we found that before any action was taken 172 had become casualties and 200 could not be traced, so that we had some slight doubts as to the efficacy of the review made every month. Then I went on to say:
Canada has no objection to an increase in total percentage of commissions; on the contrary, it welcomes it. It believes that the "merit system" on graduation brings out leaders far more effectively than the "quota system". Furthermore, it considers that the procedure now in effect for commissioning overseas will raise the standard of all R.C.A.F. aircrews, both commissioned and n.c.o. rank. The fact that a commission may be won, irrespective of quota or establishment will provide all the incentive, improvement of morale and consequent efficiency stressed so forcibly in your paragraphs 6 and 7.
Then I go on:
.	.	. it is suggested that our standard of
qualifications for commissions is being lowered, with which we do not agree.
Then with respect to another paragraph:
Canada agreed at the conference of June, 1942, to set up standards instead of commissioning all aircrews, and will loyally abide by its agreement, unless in the meanwhile it can persuade its partners, or w-hat we think more likely, they themselves of their own initiative put into practice their own theory that "all aircrews commissionable are to be * commissioned." instead of persisting in the belief that an arbitrary figure of 50 per cent is an immutable law.
The final paragraph in the United Kingdom memorandum is this, and I really think it must have been written by somebody who did not have much of an idea of Canadian public opinion. I am sure it was not written by a high official of the air ministry, because we do get on extremely well with them:
For the foregoing reasons the R.A.F. feel it necessary to maintain existing proportions on graduation. It is entirely for Canada to decide what proportion should be granted in the Royal Canadian Air Force and, whatever may be decided, Canadian authorities may count on loyal collaboration of the air ministry and R.A.F. It is only right to point out, how-ever, that if the Canadian decision results in grant in R.C.A.F. of a substantially higher total percentage of commissions than in the R.A.F., then (apart from considerations already mentioned) belief may grow up in the R.A.F. that the R.C.A.F. are adopting a substantially lower standard of commissioning Whether or not

War Appropriation-Air Services
this were true, result would be a lowering of the prestige of commissioned rank in the R.C.A.F., with consequent adverse effects on existing spirit of cordial cooperation.
The natural answer to that is, "So what?" During the course of my discussions, however, I have learned some diplomacy.
Would the minister permit a question at this point?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I first read my reply?
Yes, do.
I was going to ask the minister if he could tell us how many matriculated students there are in each of the two air forces.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not the faintest idea.
I think that would have a bearing on this question; how many graduates in arts or science also.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have it approximately, so far as we are concerned.
I think you will find that we are very much higher.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In answer to this last paragraph I said:
We desire to express the deepest appreciation for the assurance given that the Canadian authorities may count on the loyal collaboration of the air ministry and of the R.A.F. in whatever action it may take with respect to the proportion of Canadian graduates of the B.C.A.T.P. who may be commissioned.
We are confident that the standard we have Bet is such as to ensure that those commissioned will have the capacity to measure up to their responsibilities in an efficient and satisfactory manner, and we therefore feel no great anxiety with regard to any repercussions which the implementing of the Canadian method may have on the personnel of the R.A.F. generally.
The battle is still on, I may tell hon. members; we are still continuing the fight.
Don't surrender too quickly.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Well, I did give in as far as I could. I cannot go further, but I have kept on battling to try to get a hundred per cent commissions.
Suppose members of aircrew are brought down over enemy territory and taken prisoner; would the minister say on what basis the commissions are granted or the promotions continued?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That part of the agreement reads:
The commission will take effect from the date of the original recommendation by the commanding officer of the unit or, if the recommendation has not been made by the commanding
officer, from the date of the recommendation by R.C.A.F. Overseas Headquarters, even if the candidate has become a casualty by the time the recommendation is approved.
I do not know that that will work out very well. It might not have worked out well, for instance, before we started really going to town on this commissioning policy, and when there were no recommendations from the commissioning officers. There would be taken into consideration the recommendation made when the boy graduated from the school in Canada-let us say in 1941. That is what we are attempting to do in some way, when we cannot get trace of them. At least we require a recommendation by his commanding officer, even though it may not be his commanding officer on operations. That is something he has on his file. If we can put that into effect it could have a retroactive effect on a great many of those who are now prisoners of war. But the difficulty is not there. The difficulty is that, in spite of repeated telegrams, I have not been able to find out whether or not Germany wholly recognizes any notification by transferring from Stlag which, I believe, is the camp for non-commissioned officers, to Offlag, which is the camp for officer prisoners. I have not been able to find out whether they recognize promotions of which they are notified after a man has become a prisoner of war. I can say that the Italians refused to recognize this. I happened to see a dispatch dealing with that matter, representations made by the British government to the Italian government, to the effect that they should recognize these promotions and commissions, because the Germans did. And I promptly sent, or had the Department of External Affairs send, a cable, saying, "What ho! who told you the Germans did?" I have not had an answer yet, and that happened some months ago.
In no case has a prisoner been promoted unless the promotion was recommended before the capture?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is correct.

The minister deserves every support, and I believe the committee to-day has shown pretty well that it is behind him in his policy. I asked the question about the number of matriculated students and university graduates, knowing something about educational conditions in Great Britain and in this country, and how difficult it is for the average boy in England-even more difficult than in Scotland-either to get as far as matriculation in a secondary school, or subsequently to attend university, and how relatively simple it is in this country for a boy

War Appropriation-Air Services
who has the desire and the grit to make that progress. I am perfectly well aware that the depression in the early thirties enabled us to have a larger number of young men with higher education than was possible in Great Britain for boys from homes on the same income level. I think the argument of the British may apply to the British situation- although I doubt it much, because they are probably following tradition. There has been a tradition in Great Britain for years that even in cricket, for example, two teams may play in exactly the same way, but one might be termed gentlemen and the other merely players. That distinction remains throughout. It appears in the military institutions, and I imagine it is carried into the air force too.
The minister is to be congratulated. Most of us last year, when we heard him speak about the Canadianization of the air force, which subject he developed on the floor of the house, felt that he was doing an excellent job. I know that this group is glad to support him. As one who has the greatest possible regard for the old land, but who understands the class distinctions over there, and' the way in which they are perpetuated, I think the sooner we have complete control of our own Canadian air force, the better it will be for Canada and for our relations with Great Britain herself.
Then, if I may allude to one other point while I am on my feet. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) is in his seat, and he will recall that while we were at a bomber station in Great Britain a year ago last November we were approached, not by sergeants, but by commissioned officers, and were asked by them if we would use our good offices when we returned to London and came back to Canada to see to it that a common mess could be provided, where sergeant pilots, sergeant observers and so on could meet the pilot officers and other commissioned'officers. To our boys over there it was distinctly irksome that the men who flew together and fought together, and sometimes died together, the moment they alighted from their planes wTere separated into two different messes. That suggestion, made by officers we met in England, enters into this very discussion. The men themselves want to see this distinction erased. I say to the minister that I hope he will go all out, and that he will have good results in the end.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There is one other very
strong argument used by our opposite numbers in the Royal Air Force. I did refer at the conference to the idea of a joint mess. The matter was discussed, and I gathered from
Mr. Coldwell.l
what wras said that they had such a thing in the middle east command, and I think in India. I do not know how far we got with it-perhaps we did not get very far. The strongest argument used by the air ministry is this:	They say that one does not give
commissions for risk taken, for hazards, or for bravery. They say that one gives decorations for bravery; one could win the Victoria Cross. Commissions in their opinion are not given on those grounds, and it is their belief that to give commissions to all aircrew would be making them a kind of supermen.

They pretty nearly are
supermen.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Well, I am just stating their argument. They say we would be making supermen of these men whose duty it is to get into an aeroplane, fly away, fight the enemy, come back and be heroes. They do not put it in exactly those terms, but that is the gist of it. They point out further that if we did that we should take all the crew of a tank, and have them commissioned and, going beyond that, we should extend it to all members of the crew of a submarine-and so on down the list, I do not wish the committee to get the idea that they have not what appear to them to be pretty strong arguments. . In the memorandum I received they point out that a man has duties other than his flying duties. I take exception to that, and say most of the boys in the flying squadrons do not do much more than take part in their sortie, and come back and rest. The boys in the fighter squadrons are not on such long operations.
I wish the committee to understand that in these discussions with the United Kingdom we have reached the point where we can be argumentative without being enemies, and where we can discuss and put forward our views in a straightforward, honest, and frank manner without being acrimonious. My personal relations with those on the other side, and the members of the air council, are of the happiest. It is just a straight difference of opinion; I think, based upon a difference in temperament, character and upbringing. That is about the size of it. We have to stick to our own side of the question. We have taken this point of view, and I think we should stick with it. Of course if they do not wish to change their point of view. I do not see why they should be forced to do so. I must say however that we caused them some embarrassment.

Would the minister say
how the United States system is working out?

War Appropriation-Air Services
He said that they had some intermediate rank between their commissioned officers and top sergeants.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes; it is generally thought that the Americans commission more widely than other countries. As a matter of fact they do not. One of the things, I believe, which influenced the conference was the fact that the Americans were getting away more and more from what might be called wholesale commissioning, or the commissioning of everybody. They were going in the opposite direction from that in which we were going. I think in their permanent force, their prewar or pre-Pearl Harbor force, they commissioned a much greater percentage of pilots, navigators and bombers than they do now. At the present time they commission only a percentage of their pilots, not 100 per cent, and a number of others are made flight something or other, it may be flight officer, but I cannot remember the name. They are on probation for three months' active service, and possibly longer if they do not make the grade or if they are serving at home. Navigators who must work harder to pass their examinations are commissioned 100 per cent. The percentage of bombardiers who are commissioned is less. I have not these figures at the moment but I shall place them on Hansard later. Their gunners or wireless operators are not commissioned at all, they are enlisted men. Their flight engineers, of which we are starting to have some and about which we have not yet come to any agreement with regard to commissioning, are I believe all enlisted men.
If any members of the committee saw the picture "Air Force" which was exhibited here recently and which gave the details of the flight of an aircraft which flew a fabulous number of miles from San Francisco to Hawaii, from Hawaii to Wake Island, from Wake Island to the Philippines and from the Philippines to Australia, will remember that the crew consisted of a pilot officer, a second pilot officer, a navigator officer, a wireless operator air gunner who was an enlisted man, an air gunner who was an enlisted man and who was very cross because he had been remustered from a pilot, as some of them have been here, and a flight engineer who was a sergeant of twenty years' experience.
I have the figures here which were obtained from the air attache and from the United States army, and they indicate that they do not commission as great a percentage of their aircrew as we do. The same thing applies to the German air force which commissions a smaller number than either the R.A.F. or the
R.C.A.F. The French air force when it existed consisted to a large extent of noncommissioned officers. I have taken the trouble to get some comparisons. These are not strictly accurate but they will give some information to the committee and I shall place them on Hansard as soon as I find them.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations with respect to the matter under discussion, but before doing so I join with the other hon. members who have extended their congratulations to the minister upon the comprehensive and exhaustive review he has given of the operations of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Like many other districts, the district which I represent has given a substantial number of personnel to the R.C.A.F. and in common with many other districts has suffered a substantial number of casualties. To those who have been bereaved I extend my sincerest sympathy.
There is one item with respect to pay and allowances to which I wish to refer. I have two cases in mind of wives of pilot officers. The one wife is working for the civil service of Canada while the other is a member of the women's division of the R.C.A.F. In each case the pilot officer has assigned $50 per month to his wife. As I say, the one wife is employed in the civil service and receives a salary of approximately $95 a month. She also receives a marriage allowance of $45 a month, which gives her a total income of $190 a month. In the second case the wife has received a B classification in the women's division of the R.C.A.F. and is paid $1.30 per day, or $39 per month. I am not unmindful of the fact that the wife working for the civil service must provide herself with lodging and board and a certain amount of clothing, which would be a matter of expense. There appears to me to be discrimination in connection with the incomes received by the wives of these two officers who are serving in a similar capacity. The one has a total income of $190 a month while the other is receiving only $89 a month. I am of the opinion that in cases where the wife of a member of any branch of our forces enlists she should get the marriage allowance. I understand that in the Royal Air Force the dependent's allowance for a wife without other dependents amounts to four shillings a day, or about $30 a month. There is no distinction in that country between a wife serving in the women's division of the R.A.F. and one employed by the civil service or in some other capacity. I do not know to what extent attention has been given to this matter, but I trust that full consideration will be given these representations.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The question of women in the forces generally, that is, army, navy and air, receiving a dependent's allowance on enlistment, is a matter which has been considered seriously by the three services for some time past. There is now before the government for consideration, and I hope early adoption, a submission that the wives of members of the forces should retain their dependents' allowances upon appointment or enlistment to any women's division, to the same extent as if they were employed by the civil service at a salary and bonus of $3,000 or less per annum. As the committee knows, at one time women in the civil service whose husbands were in the forces were obliged to abandon their allowances or give up their jobs, but that system was abolished. The armed forces have been trying to get the same consideration for women in their divisions as is given to women in the civil service, and I have every reason to believe that the suggestion will be adopted.
Is it the treasury board that, is holding it up?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not want to blame them for everything.

This item which relates to pay and allowances was before the committee last year. At that time the minister made a statement and I quoted the discussion which had taken place in the British House of Commons in connection with this question of sovereignty. There are some Canadians who prefer to serve in the Royal Air Force. We had it in the last war. The whole scheme as operated then was that Canadians served in the Royal Air Force. There was no Royal Canadian Air Force then. The Royal Air Force had a headquarters in the city of Toronto, and trained 16,000 pilots and air mechanics. Now a change has come. We have a dual and a duplicate system.
The present minister is a child of the House of Commons; that is what Mr. Churchill called himself, or, as Mr. Churchill also put it, a servant of the House of Commons. It is a great credit to him. His father, too, was a member of the house. No matter to what party an hon. member belongs he knows that if he writes to the minister on any matter, the minister will give him full information to the best of his ability. I hope he will follow the same practice in the course of this discussion on commissions, a discussion which, in my opinion, is of no benefit to the empire training scheme. There should be no division in this matter, no attempt at and no emphasis on status or a divided sovereignty. From this point of view I am opposed to separate Canadian squadrons. Some people believe in

separate squadrons, but I am not convinced that we are following the best practice. For instance, I believe that the right way to win the war and to get the best results for money spent is to adopt a system which will not overemphasize the educational test. Education is not everything in the equipment of an air officer.
Consider, too, how we are distributing commissions. There are in this branch no fewer than 5,459 civilians or men who have received commissions from the government without any prior war training. In addition to that, forty-one press officers have been given commissions, though very few have any training in air force work.
I contend that the empire air scheme can be used as a means of uniting this empire as it was never united before, not only during the present war but for what will happen after the battle.
When this item was under discussion last year, many inequalities were disclosed in the printed schedule or blueprint which the minister laid on the table of the house. Without any very evident reason, some had got commissions while others had to be satisfied with the rank and pay of sergeants. I believe too much attention is paid to the application of an educational test on entrance in the air scheme. Beurling could not qualify under those conditions; he, and many like him, had to go overseas at their own expense to enlist.
I wish to compliment the minister upon having a splendid assistant. He adopts the same principle as his chief, in giving the members of the house information about the department. He is one of the most learned men in Canada, and one of the best informed on modern warfare, and a fine soldier himself. He knows what this empire means and what we are fighting for. I have personal reason to thank him for what he has done in connection with one or two matters I took up with him last week.
The estimated expenditure this year on pay and allowances is $238,000,000 as against $148,000,000 last year, an increase of $89,000,000. This additional amount should be sufficient to take care of existing inequalities. Let me tell the minister that nothing has caused more dissatisfaction in all the armed forces than inequalities of pay, because this is a citizens' army, and I may add that few hon. members knew inequalities existed until the minister laid on the table last session a blueprint showing the pay of all ranks from the lowest right up to the top-pay, subsistence allowance and for two to four children and dependency. The inequalities extend to overseas men as well.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Arising out of what the minister said about commissions, I should like to see some allowance made to those young men who, without waiting on the outcome of the division of opinion as to whether we should maintain a separate staff and display our sovereignty in connection with the armed forces before this began and after, went overseas at their own expense, entered the ranks and got commissions in the United Kingdom. I contend that their out-of-pocket expenses should be refunded to them or to their parents, since they incurred a good deal of expense in getting overseas and taking their training. It would be a kind and, indeed, efficient action; it woidd also be only just to those who did not wait for the war to break out or for the establishment of any empire training scheme, but went over, some in cattle-boats, some with less than the educational requirements for commissions, and worked their way right up to the top of the ladder. In this connection we might bear in mind what other countries are doing. In Germany and in Russia, after many of their generals failed, what did they do? They went out and got civilian generals almost literally off the street. Some of them were called in from commercial pursuits and not only given commissions but put in command of units. I have in mind a speech delivered in the British House of Commons by a very fine soldier and distinguished member of the house, Major Markiand, who returned from active service to take part in the debate on this particular subject. It is possible in Canada during the commission test to go too far in emphasizing the importance of educational requirements.
For a long time the department suffered in the city of Toronto from a sort of dual control wielded by the air force and by the civil service commission, and there was considerable complaint about inequalities in pay and allowances. However, the present minister has gone into the matter, and I had a letter from the chairman of the civil service commission stating that a satisfactory arrangement had been worked out whereby civilian workers, except in some very minor cases, were being appointed by the commission.
Inequalities in pay are, however, still continuing. I have already referred to the 5,459 officers reported in return No. 394. I have nothing but praise for the air scheme and system as a whole; it is one of the most glorious achievements in the history of the empire and has done a great deal to hold the empire together. But I cannot understand why it has been necessary to commission 5.459 civilian officers. They are distributed in
part as follows: headquarters-430; No. 1 training command-1,148; No. 2 training command-623; No. 3-647; No. 4-577; eastern command headquarters-135; other units of the eastern command-526; western command-161; other units-281; overseas-565. Yet there are others doing good service with a much lower rank and pay. For instance, L.A.C.s, group A. $2.25; group B, $2; group C. $1.75; others, $1.50.
Return No. 216 relates to pay and allowances. It gives a list of forty-one pres liaison officers and others engaged in the department, very few of them with any military experience whatever, who wear a uniform and get commissions and officers' pay. It states that they are entitled to "actual out-of-pocket expenses while absent from Ottawa." That may mean anything. A man may be in England; he may be travelling to Australia; he may be going to some other place. One went all over the world at a great cost. I think the committee is entitled to know in more detail what these allowances of rank are.
In conclusion, I wish to say that the work which the department has been doing this last year will write one of the most glorious pages in Canada's war record. Three or four weeks have been taken up in debating the army appropriation. I do not think so long will be occupied with the minister's department. But let me point out that, if the principle which I raised here in connection with pay and allowances in the debate of 1941, and again in 1942, had been carried out, seventy per cent of the questions which hon. members have had occasion to raise on the war appropriation bill could have been answered daily on the orders of the day. The matter can be stated in just a few sentences, and I placed it on Hansard in 1941 and early in 1942. In a new book on parliamentary procedure published last summer by G. F. M. Campion, second clerk assistant of the British House of Commons, now Clerk, and knighted, there appears the following: from a textbook which is almost as good as that of our own Clerk:
Not later than three o'clock the question hour begins. This is a more important item of business than any yet described. It is expected *to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions "turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service." (Lowel, i.332.) Their chief object is "the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events", and "they are often arranged by the government itself, so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way.

War Appropriation-Air Services
(Redlieh, ii, 241 and 242.) They are "serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers." (Todd. 1982, ii. 85.) And finally, "Questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity." (Marriott, i. 571.)
Under our standing order 1, in all cases not provided for in our rules, the usages and customs of the British house shall be followed. I am quite certain that it is a member's right to ask pertinent questions of a minister on the orders of the day being called. The last time this question was before the house the Clerk gave that opinion to a committee revising the rules, and I suggest that, if that opportunity had been accorded us, seventy per cent of the time taken up by the three ministers in answering questions on the war appropriation bills could have been eliminated. Instead of that we have only one opportunity a year on this particular bill for appropriations.
I wish to compliment the minister upon the explanation he has given. In my opinion there should be an amendment to these educational tests now that we have high-school cadets. They are leaving school at sixteen and seventeen years of age to work on the farms, and they cannot have the educational tests that were given in the early days of the war to those entering the air force and going into the manning pools. There should be an amendment along this line, applicable to these recruits, because after all this is a voluntary organization, a citizens' army, and one in which the people of Canada have taken a great deal of interest and of which they are justly proud, and they are interested in it not merely on account of what the air force is doing in this war but on account of the service it will render afterwards to keep the empire together.

Would the minister care to make a statement with regard to complaints reaching some members, including myself, on the subject of leave of absence granted to men who are fighting in Great Britain or other parts of the world? Complaints have reached me that there is a difference in the length of time of flights which an airman makes from Great Britain over France, depending upon whether he is a bomber or a fighter. For instance, I had a letter last week from a young airman who has been about two years in England and has made many flights over France and Germany. He is a fighter pilot. He states that up to the present he has done about thirty-two flights. Had he been a bomber, he says, he would have been given leave of absence
[Mr. Church.)
to come back to Canada when he had thirty flights to his credit. He wonders whether, when one makes four flights in one night, those flights are counted as four or whether they are counted merely as one trip. Could the minister make a statement as to the procedure? How long must one of our airmen remain over there before he gets leave of absence, and how many flights has he to make over Germany or France before he is granted that leave?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Usually the sortie or mission of the fighter pilot is from half an hour to three-quarters of an hour, whereas the same kind of job of the bomber is from eight to ten hours. They have operational tours. I am not at liberty to state what length of time must be flown to complete an operational tour but certainly there are much fewer sorties in a bomber than in a fighter. Rules are laid down as to how many sorties shall constitute an operational tour for bombers, for fighter pilots, for coastal command, for army cooperation and so on. After an operational tour, the personnel obtain two weeks leave of absence and then are usually posted to an operational training school for about six months and sometimes are returned to make another operational tour. That is about all the information I can give at the moment.

I should like to ask a question in regard to agricultural leave. I have received complaints with regard to No. 7 I.T.S., Saskatoon, in connection with applications for agricultural leave. Early in March application forms were made available for the men there who wished to apply for agricultural leave. I believe the leave is six weeks. Applications were sent out, and nothing further was heard about the matter until an order was issued refusing all leave in that particular station. I refer to air force administrative order A 24-5.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will the hon. member read the order?
I have not it here. A general order was sent out that no leave should be given to the personnel of No. 7, I.T.S.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is aircrew?
Yes. It is an initial training station.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are aircrew?

Yes. I should like to know why individual applications were not considered on their merits instead of a blanket order being issued refusing any leave for

War Appropriation-Air Services
these men, particularly in view of the fact that they had been given to believe, inasmuch as they were supplied with these application forms, that the cases would be dealt with on their merits.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
