speechtext: At the present time I am keeping all the aircrew I can, and I will for the rest of the war. If a man is in the aircrew, he is not going to be a farmer and he will not get leave. I am not giving farm leave to aircrew. There is to be no extension of farm leaves for ground crew beyond two months. If anyone wants an extension, if he is ground crew and is not valuable otherwise, not a man on whom we have spent $10,000, he will either be in the air force or be a farmer. He will take his discharge if he wants more than two months, but I am not running an air force to go farming, but to fight overseas and to train here. If a man enlists in the aircrew he enlists of his own free will and he must go through the training for a most important job of work, costing us $25,000 if he is a pilot, $27,000 or $28,000 if he is an observer or navigator and so on. I do not think we can afford to let him go away on farm leave. I do not know whether the committee will agree with me, but so long as I have anything to do with the air force, either it will be an air force or they will be farmers and will go back to their farms. I do not wish to have a double-barrelled organization, running farms and an air force at the same time.
That is all very well, and I am not disputing that statement. But I wish to know why these men were given application forms, and six weeks later this general order came through.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Probably because I changed the order some time in the last month or so. I am sorry, but I changed the order. It had reached the point where we had to lay down the rule that aircrew were not to be given farm leave, and that rule was laid down. I suppose it affected some particular men who had put in their application before. Whatever rule or regulation is made is bound to affect.somebody who is a border-line case. I suppose that some discretion might have been allowed or a warning given, but probably I did not think of it. Perhaps I am to blame for that.
That order just applies to aircrew and not to ground crew securing leave.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Ground crew obtain leave on application to their commanding officer,
but if they apply for an extension after two months we usually tell them: You had better stay home and farm.

I asked the minister a question a while ago about the inequality in flying pay between the commissioned officer and the non-commissioned officer in the aircrew. As the matter now stands, the officer receives two dollars a day flj'ing pay, while the non-commissioned officer in the same crew, doing exactly the same work, and often in charge of the ship, receives only seventy-five cents a day. I have heard a great deal of complaint about that. The crew perform similar duties; they are aboard the same ship, all contributing equally in the work of the ship; yet there is this difference made in flying pay. I can understand a difference in pay so far as rank is concerned, but it does seem unfair that the commissioned officer and the non-commissioned officer should not be on the same footing so far as flying pay is concerned. I know the interest which the minister shows in the men, who honour him as their minister, and I would suggest that he give consideration to this matter.
The minister said a while ago, in answer to the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that there should be an aircrew mess, that that was being done in the east. As I understand it, the Australian air force has adopted that system and it has been a great contribution to morale among the crews to meet as equals in a common mess when they return from their tours of duty.
I also wish to say a word in regard to the women in the Royal Canadian Air Force and in the other services. As I understand the regulations, any woman who joins the air force and theretofore was in receipt of a dependents' allowance is immediately deprived of it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I just answered that a
moment ago.

I appreciate that, but it seems unjustified. I would like to know from the minister whether the intention this year is to increase the scope of activities of the women in the air force. I remember very well bringing this matter up in March, 1941, and suggesting to the Minister of National Defence the need of mobilizing the women of this country. He told me at that time that not more than fifteen hundred women could possibly be employed in the army. But with the passing months and years that estimate has been greatly exceeded. To-day, while we pay

War Appropriation-Air Services
tribute and deserved tribute to the men in the air force, we ought also to pay tribute to the women who to-day are serving not only in the air force but in the other armed services.
There is a matter which I had not intended to mention, but I feel that the members of this house owe it to the women in the armed services of this country to protect their names from calumny which all too frequently is indulged in. These women are giving of their best, and while they are honoured generally throughout the country there are some persons who indulge in slander against them. I personally feel that there is one way in which this unjustified slander could be and should be terminated, and that is by a series of prosecutions being taken under the defence of Canada regulations against the rumour-mongers. All of us have occasion to see the wohderful work that these women are doing in the air force and in the other services, and we as members and as Canadians owe it to them to uphold their good name and to assure those who dare to scandalize them that they will be fittingly punished. I suggest to the minister and to the other heads of the defence department that a few prosecutions would put an end to -what is all too frequently the contribution of some people who seem to have nothing better to do than to cast aspersions on the good names of those who serve.

I have a question to ask the minister in reference to pay and allowances in connection with the fleet air arm. The minister may have said something about it while I was out. If he has not, I shall be glad to get this information. I know a number of young men, highly educated, who have gone over to England recently and joined the fleet air arm. They are young lads less than nineteen years of age. Apparently they enlist one day and within a day or two afterwards are on the way to England. I understand that when they return they go down to the southern states for further training. If the minister is familiar with this-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the fleet air arm. I have not the faintest idea about that. That comes under the navy, and my.hon. friend will have to ask the minister for naval services.

Then I will ask about pay and allowances on the navy estimates.
There is another matter on which I wish to say a word. The papers to-day publish the decorations that have been well earned by Canadians. I notice that Mr. and Mrs. Deutscher of Odessa, who have eight sons in

the Royal Canadian Air Force, were recently honoured at an outdoor gathering. They deserved it. Has any consideration been given to recognizing those parents who are giving a large number of sons to the armed services? There is a Scotch family in my riding, living at 82 Harvie avenue, Mr. and Mrs. David Seggie, who have seven sons in the armed services; and if any consideration is being given to recognizing in some way parents who have given so many sons to the armed services, this family might be considered. Of course I know it can be said that a family with only one son are contributing much because they are giving their all. Nevertheless I feel that the father and mother of seven or eight or nine sons in the armed services deserve some sort of recognition.

The minister was very frank and as explicit as we could expect in regard to the commissioning of our pilots overseas. Might I ask if he could give any more information on the procedure which is being adopted? Are the deficiencies, if I may call them that, in the commissioned ranks of the boys who have been over there for some time being made up by reason of this periodical two-months' review of their record? I understand that the Royal Air Force authorities, in conjunction with Royal Canadian Air Force headquarters overseas, review the record of a man who has been overseas for more than two months. Once they do that; once the case is reviewed by the two authorities, is there a further automatic review every two months or six months? Then the other method of getting a commission is by the member of aircrew making his own application, when he is not recommended by his commanding officer. Are both these systems working, or is one not effective? Just how is the whole matter of rectifying the situation, as we see it, being handled?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think both systems are working. We have liaison officers in, I think, six different districts in Great Britain, and of course in addition we have a headquarters in Cairo. Probably we shall have one in India before long and possibly also one in North Africa. They are intensely interested in going ahead with this commissioning. Our liaison officers visit stations wherever there are Canadians in the Royal Air Force or in Canadian squadrons, and by that means we are pushing forward these commissions. I gather from the air ministry that they are doing their best to bring them to the attention of the officers w'ho finally pass upon them. Then last November, as I said a moment ago, we hit upon a plan of handing to the air

War Appropriation-Air Services
ministry nine hundred names of men who had been recommended, and said, "What about it? These fellows were recommended on graduation. Why don't you give them their commissions?" They have been looking for some of those men ever since. We have also hit upon another plan, of going right back to the inception of the training plan, and every one who has had 60-60-70 is given a commission. That is one way of getting more of them in. Usually we do consult the authorities, to see whether or not there is anything against a man, but we are commissioning back as quickly as we can in that way, so that we are making up for a good many who are of the backlog. With the representations we are making I think perhaps the provision with respect to personal application for a commission will not be so necessary as it appeared to be a year ago, when it was first introduced.

In order that the review provision and also the personal application may not become dead letters, is there a special section of the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas set up .to deal just with those matters?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; but we have a personnel section overseas which deals with all the interests of our personnel. I do not think a week goes by without my reminding the air officer in command overseas that he has a job to perform in getting commissions through for our 'boys over there. This seems to be one of the important things we do, to stir up our own people and have them stir up the air ministry. I can assure my hon. friend we are just camping on their trail as constantly as we can.

Then may I ask a question in regard to the marks of the boys who are now going through. As I understand it, the total marks are in three classifications; for ground work or theory, for actual flying, and for character and leadership.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. The third1 classification used to be called, "officer qualities," but we changed it to "character and leadership."
Is that simply a matter of what an officer thinks of a man from his observation, or has it to do with anything written? It is pretty much a matter of opinion, I suppose.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I could send my hon. friend a copy of form 211, which covers both sides of a very long page. It has to do with a man's aptitude, his initiative, how he acts, whether he does things without being pushed to do
them, whether he gets along well with his fellow men, whether he does this, that and the other thing.
It sounds pretty scientific.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think it was made up by a man who was employed by one of the large insurance companies for the purpose of checking on personnel and by an officer by the name of Chant.

I think there is a
psychology professor by that name.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe he is a psychologist, and if I am not mistaken he was employed by one of the large insurance companies at Hartford. In any event, he had been doing this sort of work for an insurance company and, with the assistance of others, he drew up this form 211. I have no objection to showing it to anyone in the house. It is a complicated affair, but I am told, that it does bring results.
Perhaps hon. members would not succeed in that test any more than the minister succeeded in the other one.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are a great many of my hon. friends who would not succeed on that test, I am sure; there are questions with regard to sociability, politeness, garrulousness. All the prominent characteristics of members of this house, as well as the general public, would be checked and marked. There are a great many to whom I would not give a commission under form 211.

Perhaps the minister would answer a couple of questions which were asked yesterday. The first was, why does the air force not pay the members of the women's division the same pay as men for equal work? The other question was why dependents of members of the women's division are not given dependents' allowances.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In reply to the second question, that is under way, and I confidently expect that within a few days it will be settled. In regard to the first question, I really do not know' why we do not give the same rate of pay to women. Originally in both the army and the air force women were paid two-thirds the basic male pay. I do not know where it came from, but I am told we followed the example of Great Britain. In any event, the suggestion now up for consideration is that the basic rate of pay for women be increased to four-fifths, or eighty per cent. I made some inquiry in the matter just before I came here to-day, and I am told that this is the ratio between men and women

War Appropriation-Air Services
in Great Britain. What that has to do with us, I do not know, but someone hit on that. Then the question arose as to trades pay, and some of us took a very strong stand that if a woman were performing the work of a man in a trade, at least she should get the same trade pay; she was getting only two-thirds before that. A man doing a job as parachute packer in our lot, say, would not be as good at that job as a woman, but he would be getting twenty-five or fifty cents trades pay, whatever it might be, while the woman would be getting only two-thirds of that. We have made representations that the women be put on a level with the men so far as trades pay is concerned. I think the provisions of the new pay schedule for women will be: first, a raise from two-thirds to four-fifths of what is paid the men; second, full trades pay for the work done; third, dependents' allowances, just the same as though the woman were employed in the civil service or in any civilian capacity.

Has the minister any
idea when these new rates of pay may come into effect?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They should come in soon, because the matter has been hanging for a long time.

I should like to ask the minister if our men in the R.C.A.F. overseas are able to draw the full pay and allowances of their rank now, or is the situation the same as it was some time ago, that they are paid on the basis of the R.A.F. pay?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We are still deferring pay. I think, however, when the boys go on leave they are allowed to draw a portion of their deferred pay.

Perhaps it would not be
inopportune to say a word at this time about the medical service the minister has established in connection with the air force. I know something of the work of the men connected with that service, and I wish to commend him upon the splendid staff he has been able to get together under, first, the able leadership of Doctor Ryan, whose rank I am never sure of-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member is not
the only one who makes mistakes of that kind. The minister does not know all the ranks yet.

I believe Doctor Ryan was
air commodore. I believe Air Commodore Ryan was the first medical officer wrho assisted the minister in the development of a medical service for the air force. Then, when he left

he was followed by Air Commodore Tice, who is the very worthy succesor of Air Commodore Ryan. In that service we also have Professor Best who, I believe, is a squadron leader- or has he gone higher than that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know.

And there are a great many others, including Doctor Tisdale and Doctor Clark Noble, who are doing extraordinarily good work in connection with the scientific side of flying.
I do not think the public realizes fully what that service means. It is a highly specialized part of medicine. For the last two or three years some of these men have been undertaking scientific research in various parts of Canada, and the results of their efforts have led to a great improvement, not only in detecting men who are incapable of flying, but in developing methods which will improve the efficiency of the flying service. I do not think any words of mine could too gTeatly exaggerate the great value of the scientific contribution made by the medical service for air.
I have heard1 criticism from some parts of the house about there being three medical services. Well, there may be some merit in the criticism-I am not prepared to express an opinion at the moment. I can conceive of there being one head and three branches, for the air, the navy and the army. There might be efficient coordination, if that were done. But at any rate, starting from scratch, the minister has developed a medical service in his air force which is second to none anywhere.
I regret I was not present in the house the other evening when the minister made his first presentation. I wish to commend him upon his admirable report, and the frank manner in which it was given. I am sure the development of the air training plan has met with the approval of the majority of people in Canada, certainly the majority of those with whom I have talked. I always think that frankness has its own reward, and hon. members feel when they question the minister that they receive an honest, straight and quick reply.

I should like to express my appreciation of the splendid work the minister has done in connection with the air training plan. Some little time ago I placed on the order paper some questions which related specifically to the recognition by way of promotion for merit of radio technicians in the Royal Canadian Air Force who are serving overseas. On that occasion the minister said that he would be pleased if the question could

In connection with this matter I would quote briefly from a letter which, I believe, covers the matter I have in mind. This letter was received only a short time after my questions were placed on the order paper. It states:
As a member of the R.C.A.F. enlisted as a radio technician or "radio D.F. mechanic", as they are now called, I would like to bring to your attention certain facts regarding conditions in this branch of the R.C.A.F. .	.	.
While writing as an individual, I may state that my views expressed here are shared by a large number of people, both within and outside the R.C.A.F. These views are certainly those of the majority of radio technicians. As one of a group of 500 here waiting posting to Clinton, Ontario, I have been able to discuss the subject with a large number of them, and most of them feel the same way as I do on this matter.
Our main grievance is the lack of promotion in the R.C.A.F., once we complete our course and go on active duty. Our course is one of *the hardest in the R.C.A.F., consisting of eighteen weeks study on radio principles at a university, and then courses on radio-location at Clinton, Ontario. Those passing the examinations at the end of the university course are reclassified from A.C.2 to L.A.C. and also get "B" trades pay, so that their pay increases from $1.30 to $2 a day. The Clinton course is six weeks, but approximately 50 per cent passing this course take a second course of two months. A very small percentage of those successful in the second course receive commissions. All the remainder are posted out as L.A.C.'s, "B" grouping, to active duty.
All the evidence that I have seen, both in the form of letters from radio technicians on active service, and press reports, show that we receive no further promotion. A number have obtained "A" trades pay (25 cents a day more) and a few, corporal's stripes, but the great majority remain L.A.C.'s. Many of these men are university graduates in arts or science, and a number qualified to obtain commissions in the army. They preferred the Air Force to the army, however, and being ineligible for aircrew, were told that their qualifications and education could be best used in the trade of radio technician. An examination of a list of graduates of any university who have enlisted in the R.C.A.F. shows that practically all those in any branch except radio-location work are commissioned officers, holding their rank because of their education and technical qualifications. But of those enlisted as radio technicians, 90 per cent will be found to be only L.A.C.'s.
I have personally examined the lists appearing in the quarterly issues of the McGill Alumni News and know this to be a fact as regards McGill graduates, serving in the R.C.A.F.
Radio technicians feel strongly that they are getting a "raw deal" and that either their services and abilities are not being properly recognized or that, if they cannot advance beyond the rank of L.A.C., then their talents and abilities are misplaced and could be used to better advantage elsewhere in the R.C.A.F. or in the other services. This feeling is strengthened when they see large numbers of men receiving promotions to N.C.O. ranks in other branches 72537-208
of the R.C.A.F., often soon after they have completed their courses. They see "washouts" from the radio mechanics' course remustered into other trades where they quickly obtain N.C.O. rank. If they had joined the army for radio-detection work, they could have obtained sergeant's stripes; if they had enlisted in the navy for submarine detection work (a course similar to the R.C.A.F. radio-detection work) they would have been given the rank of petty officer. The American army gives either N.C.O. or specialist "ranking to all their radio technicians. And when they find that being an L.A.C. makes them liable to fatigue and general duties and ordering around by disciplinarian N.C.O.'s, many with not half their intelligence, then they wonder why they entered the course at all. . . .
Most people with whom I have discussed this subject feel that radio mechanics should receive n.c.o. rank as corporals and sergeants following completion of their course, or they should be rated as technical n.c.o's and specialists as in the American army. Almost without exception, every member of the R.C.A.F., whether aircrew, radio technician or in some other trade, definitely believes that radio technicians are not getting their fair share of promotions in the R.C.A.F.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The matter of radio
mechanics is another matter that requires a great deal of explanation. I have a statement that I am ready to make, but I do not think I could give it inside of ten minutes. A number of hon. members are interested in these radio mechanics and there is quite a story to be told. I should like to make this statement to-morrow.
In the meantime I can answer some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre. First, he wanted to know why officers receive $2 a day flying pay when other ranks receive only seventy-five cents a day. In answering this question I may say the developed view regarding the flying pay is that it must be regarded primarily as payable for the qualifications of being graduated through a course and of being able to fly operationally as part of an aircrew and of being under continuous liability to fly. An officer meeting these qualifications receives S2 a day flying pay, whereas a sergeant pilot receives seventy-five cents a day flying pay and seventy-five cents trades pay, or a total of SI.50. The difference of fifty cents a day is attributed to the higher responsibilities devolving on an officer and the greater expense incurred by an officer in obtaining the recreational facilities which are so necessary for aircrew. The officer who sent me this communication adds what I



War Appropriation-Air Services
think is the crux of the situation when he says that the difference arising for officers and air men is a carryover from peace-time practice. I shall be ready to answer any questions dealing with pay and allowances and with aircrew even though we may pass this item to-night. However, if the committee does not wish to pass it, it is all one to me.

A moment ago I referred to Professor Best, who I wrongly stated was in the air force. He is actually in the navy, but it was an associate of his in the Banting institute, to whom I was referring, Squadron Leader Frank, who has made great progress in our knowledge of high altitude flying.

There is another matter in connection with flying pay or whatever it is called technically in the service. Certain high administrative officers get this allowance even though they do no actual flying, or certainly do not pilot planes themselves. Is this not just a hangover from olden times? Is there any justification for a man who of necessity sits behind a desk, not because of any desire I admit, still receiving this $2 a day additional? It is like some other things we sometimes come across in this parliament. For doing something people receive money which they may be entitled to when one considers the over-all picture, but are not entitled to when the specific item is considered. Perhaps the pay of these officers who are receiving this $2 flying pay should be raised.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: These officers are on what is called the general list. This list was revised some years ago, I am not certain just how long ago, and a certain number of officers who were fliers in every sense of the word and most of whom were performing duties connected with active flying although they might not actually pilot planes, were retained on the list even in peace time. Now that their duties call for more flying than they did before, it would be very difficult, in effect, to reduce their pay. They are general list officers, and they get that additional pay compared with the man who is on the non-flying list. During war time they have greater responsibilities and more work to do, and to reduce their pay would be contrary to what we have been doing generally.

Some difficulty would arise where you have a man who was in the air force in the last war and who would

not be on the general list. I know of one wing commander who has the Military Cross -he may have been in the infantry-and who is in charge of a station. He does not receive this pay, while another man with the same rank at another station does. There does not seem to be much reason to have this difference in pay to two men with the same rank and doing the same job. If this is a hangover from olden days, perhaps it could be rectified by an increase in pay to the one officer. No matter how large your air force may be in peace time, it will not be great enough to carry on during a war, and you will have to bring in additional men who may or may not be entitled to flying pay. I suppose this flying pay is paid simply because a man has his wings?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Flying pay is another thing. These are general list officers. The other is casual pay which an officer gets who is not a general list officer.
Are you on the general list if you have your wings?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I could not say. At one time either the treasury board or the minister drastically reduced the number of men on the general list. Whether the number has been increased since the war started, I could not say. I shall have to look into it and I will let my hon. friend know.

Are
the men stationed in Alaska or in the United States paid in United States funds?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know, but I shall find out. We have under consideration now the granting of an increased rate of pay to men in Alaska, but I could not say whether they are paid in United States funds.
There are some men stationed in the United States.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is some provision about those who are in the United States.

I
know the men at the legation in Washington are paid in United States funds, and then deductions are made.
